title: Matching Riders and Drivers
objective: After this level you can explain how ride and delivery apps match each request to a nearby driver and raise prices when demand spikes.
summary: Closest isn't always quickest, so ride apps match riders and drivers in batches to cut average waits; when requests outnumber drivers, surge prices rise, within legal limits.

cards.headline: Why doesn't a ride app just send the closest car?
cards.body: It used to. Uber says it first matched riders by asking "Who's closest?" and learned that closest doesn't always mean quickest. Traffic, an overpass or a river can turn a car that looks near into a long wait.

cards.headline: Matching in batches
cards.body: Now, in the seconds after you request a ride, Uber looks at nearby drivers and riders together, as one batch. Then it pairs them up to cut the average wait for everyone, not just to hand each rider the closest car. Picture two riders on the same street: giving the first one the nearest car might leave the second waiting ages. Sorting out all the pairs at once can do better for both.

cards.headline: When requests outnumber cars
cards.body: Bad weather, rush hour and big events can bring more ride requests to an area than there are drivers. That's when surge pricing switches on. Prices rise, updated in real time and different from one neighborhood to the next. The higher price is meant to pull more drivers toward the busy area, while some riders choose to wait for prices to drop. The price becomes a signal that moves cars.

cards.headline: A limit on the surge
cards.body: Surge pricing also has limits set outside the app. In July 2014 Uber agreed with New York's attorney general to cap its prices during emergencies and natural disasters, in line with the state's price-gouging law, and the rules applied nationally.

questions.prompt: Put the chain of events behind surge pricing in order.
items: Pull more drivers toward the busy area
questions.explanation: When more ride requests come in than there are drivers, surge pricing switches on, and the higher price is meant to pull more drivers toward the busy area.

questions.prompt: Why does Uber match riders and drivers in batches instead of always sending the closest car?

options.label: To cut the average wait for everyone in the batch
To give drivers longer breaks between their trips
options.rationale: The goal named is shorter average waits.

options.label: Because GPS can only locate cars in groups
options.rationale: Location isn't the limit; closest isn't always quickest.

options.label: To make every rider pay the same fare
options.rationale: Batching is about waits, not fares.

questions.explanation: Closest doesn't always mean quickest, so pairing a whole batch at once reduces the average wait for everyone.

questions.prompt: Your ride request has to cross the internet to reach the app's matching system. How does it travel?

options.label: As one unbroken message on a phone line held open just for it
options.rationale: The internet doesn't reserve a line; data is split up.

options.label: As a radio signal straight to the nearest driver
options.rationale: Requests go through the network, not directly to a car.

options.label: In small packets that travel separately and are reassembled
As a picture copied by each router
options.rationale: Routers pass along packets of numbers.

questions.explanation: Like a photo sent from a phone, the request is broken into packets that travel independently and are reassembled at the other end.
